## Iteration 56 — batch 28: the Citro3D backend places a draw with its own world matrix

Priority item **6(c)** from `docs/CONTINUATION.md`: *"the Citro3D backend ignores
`MeshDraw::world`, so the 3DS cannot place an object until it has a per-draw
matrix"* (`docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md` put it the same way: *"the 3DS has one frame-wide
MVP uniform, so per-object placement needs backend support before the 3DS
frontend binds a `ScriptRuntime`"*). This is the first game-porting batch after
six batches of harness and record work, and it is a real gap, not a tidiness
change: `mdk_render_draw_mesh` accepts a transform and the Citro3D backend threw
it away.

### What changed

* **`mdk_3ds/src/render/pica_matrix.{h,cpp}` (new).** The Citro3D matrix math,
  moved out of `renderer_c3d.cpp` into a file that compiles on a host, because
  that is the only way any of it can be pinned: the three PICA conversions each
  fail as *invisible geometry*, and the Citro3D picture is UNVERIFIED on hardware
  (AGENTS.md P6). Four functions — `isIdentity`, `eyeViewProjection`,
  `drawMatrix`, `registers`. `eyeViewProjection` is the old `buildEyeMvp` body
  **element for element and in the same order**, so the frame's per-eye matrix is
  bit-identical across the move; the multiply is the plain triple loop the Vulkan
  backend uses (`renderer_vk.cpp:690`), deliberately **not** `mdk::multiply` from
  `util/matrix.h`: that one spells `std::fma` out to be bit-exact against
  System.Numerics, and VFPv2 has no FMA, so on this target it is a libm call —
  four per element, sixteen elements, once per draw. Verified in the shipped
  object: `arm-none-eabi-objdump --disassemble=_ZN3mdk4pica…multiply…` contains
  **no `bl` at all**, and `eyeViewProjection`'s only call is to `multiply`.
* **`renderer_c3d.cpp`.** `begin_frame` now keeps the eye's matrix on the
  renderer (`r->eyeVp`) instead of building a temporary and dropping it, and
  `drawRecorded` composes each queued draw's `world` against it:
  `mdk::pica::drawMatrix(draw->world, r->eyeVp, m)`. The write is **cached**
  (`r->matrixIsFrame`), because `C3D_FVUnifMtx4x4` dirties the uniform buffer on
  every call: a frame of arena batches — every one of which carries an identity
  world — costs no multiply and no uniform write, and only an object draw pays
  one. Same shape as the cull-mode cache already in that function, and the same
  lesson the vault records twice ([[citro3d-redundant-per-draw-state-writes]],
  Turok and Perfect Dark).
* **`tests/scripts/pica_matrix_tests.{h,cpp}` (new), wired into `vm_tests`**
  *before* the game-data check, so it cannot skip on a data-less host — the same
  ordering the archive guards use and for the same reason (review-9 F1). The
  Makefile adds `-I../../mdk_3ds/src` last on the include path so it cannot
  shadow a core or Linux header.

### Why composing against the baked matrix is the same product

The two PICA conversions are right-multiplications by fixed matrices — the depth
remap is `M·E` with `E = I[E₃₂ = −1]`, the quarter turn is `M·R` with
`R[R₁₀ = 1, R₀₁ = −1]` (determinant +1) — so for any world `W`:

```
(W * V * P) * E * R  ==  W * (V * P * E * R)
```

which is what lets the conversions be baked once per frame and a per-draw world
composed against the result, instead of rebuilding the chain per draw. The
identity of the two sides is pinned by a test, not asserted here: see
`testTheWorldComposesOnTheLeftOfTheView`, which compares `drawMatrix(W,
eyeViewProjection(V,P,e))` against `eyeViewProjection(mulIndependent(W,V), P, e)`
— two association orders of one product, computed by different code.

### The second item: the diagnostic triangle was replacing the real draw's state

Found while putting the per-draw matrix into `drawRecorded`, and fixed in the
same function because the new uniform cache is entangled with it.

The diagnostic triangle ran **before** the real draw and installed its own vertex
buffer, combiner and matrix. `C3D_GetBufInfo()` hands out the **context's** single
`BufInfo` — this file calls it and never hands one back with `C3D_SetBufInfo`, so
the two calls return the same struct, and citro3d keeps render state in one global
context (the cull-mode comment in this file already says so). Drawing the triangle
first therefore replaced the buffer description the real draw had just installed,
and `C3D_DrawArrays` flushes the dirty state before drawing: the mesh's draw read
the triangle's 15 floats at the mesh's offsets. `diagnosticTriangle` is `true` by
default and nothing ever sets it false, so that was every draw, not a debug build.
The triangle now runs **last** in the draw, where it can only affect the next draw
— and every draw installs its own buffer, combiner and matrix at its top, except
the matrix, which is cached, so the cache is told (`matrixIsFrame = false`).

Recorded rather than hidden: this is a behaviour change on a target this host
cannot look at. It is a code-level defect (the aliasing is not a matter of
opinion), the fix removes state rather than adding it, and the Citro3D picture
stays UNVERIFIED either way.

### What was NOT touched, and why

* **C3D depth and blend state** (the other half of item 6(c)): `C3D_DepthTest`
  stays `GPU_ALWAYS`/no-write and there is still no `C3D_AlphaBlend`, so
  `Pass::Blended` glass is still opaque on the 3DS. That needs a projection
  remap, `C3D_DepthMap`, the test function, a clear value and a capture — a
  slice of its own, and the depth pull is meaningless while the depth test is
  off. Left as an open item.
* **Per-eye replay.** `begin_frame` sets up both eye targets but the frame's
  draws are issued once, into the last target `C3D_FrameDrawOn` installed, so
  the left eye currently gets only its clear. The vault's prior solution is
  [[citro3d-display-list-stereo-replay-non-fast3d]] — record the draw list,
  replay it per eye with a swapped view — and `DrawQueue` already *is* that
  recorded list, so the second eye is now a replay with a different `eyeVp`
  rather than a second scene walk. `r->eyeVp`'s comment says where the flush has
  to move when it lands. New open item, recorded with this evidence.
* No shipped Linux source, no shared `mdk_core` source, no golden, no gate, no
  `MeshDraw` layout change. `MeshDraw::world`'s default stays all-zeros (not

### What was implemented

The Citro3D backend now installs the oracle's depth state instead of disabling the
depth buffer.

| | before | after | oracle |
|---|---|---|---|
| depth map | `C3D_DepthMap(true, 1.0f, 1.0f)` (unused) | same three numbers, now named `pica::kDepthMap*` and load-bearing | — |
| depth test | `C3D_DepthTest(false, GPU_ALWAYS, (GPU_WRITEMASK)0)` | `GPU_LEQUAL` | `compare_op = LESS_OR_EQUAL` (`Renderer.cs:606`) |
| test enabled | never | every pass except `OnTop`/`Overlay` | `enable_depth_test = mesh && pass ∉ {Overlay, OnTop}` (`:606`) |
| depth write | never | every pass except `Blended`, `OnTop`, `Overlay` | `enable_depth_write = mesh && !blended && pass ≠ OnTop` (`:607`) |
| depth clear | `0` | `0x00FFFFFF` | the buffer's maximum, because the map stores 0 at the near plane |
| write mask | `(GPU_WRITEMASK)0` | `GPU_WRITE_ALL` / `GPU_WRITE_COLOR` | — |

* `mdk_3ds/src/render/pica_matrix.{h,cpp}` gains `DepthState`,
  `depthStateForPass(Pass)`, `storedDepth(zNdc)`, `depthPasses(state, zNdc, stored)`
  and the four named constants. The pass rule lives there for the same reason the
  matrix math does: it is host-testable and the backend is not.
* `renderer_c3d.cpp`: `installDepthState()` (cached on the renderer, the same
  shape as the cull-mode cache, because `C3D_DepthTest` dirties the effect block on
  every call), the frame install, the per-draw transition in `drawRecorded`, the
  clear value, and the diagnostic triangle now disables the test — it sits on the
  far plane, so with the scene depth-tested it would go missing in exactly the busy
  scenes it is needed for.
* `renderer_c3d.cpp` now logs the depth state once at init
  (`depth: map z*1.0+1.0 near=0.0000 far=1.0000 clear=0xffffff test=LEQUAL`).
  `storedDepth` is what produces those two numbers, so the invisible state is
  recorded by any hardware run even when nobody can see the screen (P6's only
  evidence channel).

### Prior-solution lookup (all three sources)

* **Pi knowledge (`mdk-sdl`, 3881 chunks / 936 files — the base now exists, owner

* **Obsidian vault** (read directly, read-only; no Obsidian MCP in this session).
  Three notes decided the batch:
  `60-references/3ds-platform/citro3d/01-overview-and-init.md:87-104` — citro3d's
  own default state, `C3D_DepthMap(true, -1.0f, 0.0f)` with
  `C3D_DepthTest(true, GPU_GREATER, GPU_WRITE_ALL)`, i.e. the **reversed** range,
  which is what the guide's "clearDepth = 0" advice belongs to;
  `10-projects/forsaken/findings/citro3d-renderer-architecture-and-vertex-pipeline.md:129-131`
  and `citro3d-missile-chase-cam-per-eye-scissored-clear.md:91` — **Forsaken, on this
  hardware**, pairs `C3D_DepthMap(true, 1.0f, 1.0f)` with `GPU_LESS` +
  `GPU_WRITE_ALL` and clears to `0xFFFFFF`;
  `30-architecture/patterns/pica200-ndc-z0-is-the-far-clip-plane-billboards-vanish.md`
  — the PICA's far **clip** plane is `z <= 0` in the `[-1,0]` range, so a vertex at
  exactly `z = 0` is on the boundary (recorded as an open item, not fixed: it is a
  property of the conversion the port already ships).
* **`../forsaken/3DS_PORT_NOTES.md` "Problem 1: Depth Range"** — "PICA200 depth
  hardware wants `z ∈ [-1, 0]` (near=-1, far=0)", and the native-citro3d form of the
  conversion is `_33' = _33 - 1`, `_43' = _43`, i.e. `row[2] -= row[3]`, which is
  what `pica_matrix.cpp` already does. The direction this batch installs is the one
  that conversion implies.
* **Cognee MCP is not exposed in this harness** — not consulted, and not claimed.

Two claims were measured on the linked library rather than recalled, because both
had a wrong version in circulation:

1. `C3D_DepthMap` in the installed citro3d applies **no** hidden bias:
   `arm-none-eabi-objdump -d $DEVKITPRO/libctru/lib/libcitro3dd.a`, section
   `.text.C3D_DepthMap`, is `strb r0,[r4,#233]; bl f32tof24; str r0,[r4,#224];
   vmov.f32 s0,s16; bl f32tof24; str r0,[r4,#228]` and nothing else — the two
   floats go into the effect block verbatim, so the stored depth is `z*zScale +
   zOffset`.
2. `C3D_RenderTargetClear`'s `clearDepth` is the **raw fill pattern**:
   `.text.C3D_FrameBufClear` passes it straight to `GX_MemoryFill` as the fill
   value, so `0xFFFFFF` is the 24-bit maximum under either byte order of a
   `DEPTH24_STENCIL8` word.

The choice is deliberately robust to the one thing that could not be measured. If a
future citro3d folds the old `z*0.5 + 0.5` bias back in, `(scale 1, offset 1)` over
`[-1,0]` still maps monotonically **increasing with distance** into a subset of
`[0,1]`, and `0xFFFFFF` is still the buffer's maximum — the three properties the
depth test actually needs. A sign error is not covered by that argument, and a sign
error is what `testTheRealMatrixPutsTheNearPlaneNearest` pins.

## Iteration 58 — batch 30: the draws go to the eye the panel actually shows

**Risk: high** — the frame's draw order and the whole of the 3DS's stereo path, on
the backend nobody can look at from this host (P6 open). Mitigated by measuring
citro3d's own target-selection code out of the linked library rather than reasoning
about it, and by putting the three things that can silently black the screen (the
slider clamp, each eye's sign, the mono skip) in `pica::eyePlan`, where a host test
pins them — **7 mutations, each of which turns the suite red** (table below).

### The finding, which started as last batch's open item

Batch 29 recorded, as a found-not-fixed item, that "the Citro3D backend draws **one**
pass into the last-installed eye target, so the left eye currently gets only its
clear". Checking that before continuing turned it into something larger. The order
was:

1. `mdk_render_begin_frame` looped over both eyes and called
   `C3D_FrameDrawOn(targetLeft)` then `C3D_FrameDrawOn(targetRight)`, with each eye's
   matrix in the uniform — **before a single draw existed**, because the frontend
   queues its draws between `begin_frame` and `end_frame`.
2. `mdk_render_end_frame` called `flushDraws`, i.e. every draw of the frame, into
   whatever target was current: **the right one**, with the right eye's matrix still
   in the uniform.
3. The init sets `C3D_RenderTargetSetOutput(targetLeft, GFX_TOP, GFX_LEFT, …)` and
   `main_3ds.cpp:98` calls `gfxSet3D(true)`. With the 3D slider closed the panel
   displays the **left** buffer.

So on hardware with the slider closed — the default, and the only state an emulator
without a modelled slider is ever in — the top screen showed `clear_colour` and
nothing else, and the entire scene went into a buffer nobody displays. That is not a
stereo defect, it is a black screen, and it is the reason this batch jumped the
priority order: every later 3DS item (blend, `DepthPull`, the middle 173 px) is
unevaluable behind it.

### What was measured, not recalled

`arm-none-eabi-objdump -d $DEVKITPRO/libctru/lib/libcitro3dd.a` (the library this
Makefile links):

* `.text.C3D_FrameDrawOn` is
  `strb r3(=1),[r0,#24]` (`target->active`) ; `add r0,r0,#8` ; `bl C3D_SetFrameBuf` ;
  `ldrh r3,[r4,#18]` ; `ldrh r2,[r4,#16]` ; `mov r1,#0` ; `mov r0,#0` ;
  `bl C3D_SetViewport` — and nothing else. So it **is** the target-selection call,
  it selects it for the draws that FOLLOW it, and it also resets the viewport to the
  target's own size (which is why the per-eye `C3D_SetViewport` stays: it is the
  documented place an inset would narrow it).
* `.text.C3D_SetFrameBuf` copies the 16-byte framebuffer descriptor into the context
  slot at `+0x1d8` and sets dirty bit 32 (`orr ip, ip, #32`), i.e. the GX registers
  are flushed at the next draw. A `FrameDrawOn` that is not followed by draws is
  therefore not deferred work that happens later — it is work that the next
  `FrameDrawOn` overwrites.

### What was changed

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| who selects the target | `begin_frame`, both eyes, before any draw exists | `end_frame`, one eye at a time, immediately before that eye's replay |
| how many eye passes | always 2 installed, always 1 drawn (the last) | `pica::eyePlan`: 1 with the slider closed, 2 with it open |
| the queue | flushed once at the end | `replayQueue` per eye; `queue.reset()` after the last eye |
| the eye offset | computed in `begin_frame`, `(eye==0)?-x:+x` | `pica::eyePlan(slider, separation)`, clamped, signed, host-tested |

`installEye(target, offset)` is the old loop body, unchanged in substance (target,
matrix, program, attr info, combiner, depth state, cull, depth map, viewport,
scissor). `flushDraws` keeps its old contract for the canvas and inset paths and is
now `replayQueue` + `reset`.

**Why mono draws one pass.** Forsaken, on this hardware and the same era of engine:
"Two full render passes ≈ 2× CPU+GPU cost. At ~60 fps mono this gives ~26–30 fps
stereo (measured in Mandarine). **Slider = 0 disables stereo and restores full
framerate**" (`3DS_PORT_NOTES.md`, Hardware Stereoscopic 3D). Drawing the right eye
with the slider closed is invisible work on a 268 MHz ARM11, so `eyePlan` returns
one pass. The right buffer is still cleared every frame, so opening the slider
mid-game cannot show a stale buffer.

### Falsification: seven mutations of `pica::eyePlan`

Run out of tree (`$HOME/scratch/mdk/mut30`), baseline `failures=0`:

| # | mutation | result |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | `passes = 2` → `1` (stereo never happens) | 4 failures (`junk.passes`, `flat.passes`, …) |
| E2 | the mono early-return disabled | 2 failures (`mono.passes`, `neg.passes`) |
| E3 | the two eye offsets swapped | 7 failures (every sign assertion) |
| E4 | the upper clamp removed | 2 failures — the Mandarine garbage reaches the matrix |
| E5 | the `* 0.5f` dropped (full separation per eye) | 7 failures |
| E6 | `depth <= 0` → `depth < 0` (closed slider draws stereo at zero offset) | 2 failures |
| E7 | the lower clamp moved to 0.5 | 4 failures |

What the host suite **cannot** reach is the replay structure itself (the loop in
`end_frame`, and `reset()` after the last eye rather than inside the loop). That is
stated rather than papered over: it is covered by reading, by the two builds, and by
the fact that `replayQueue` only reads the buckets. The canvas and inset flush points
still call `flushDraws`, which now runs **before** the per-eye replay; neither is
called by the 3DS frontend or the core today (`grep` for `canvas_begin`/`begin_inset`
outside the backends is empty), and `mdk_render_canvas_quad` is a no-op on this
backend, so nothing is lost — recorded as an open item for whoever lands a HUD.

## Iteration 59 — batch 31: the diagnostic draws once per eye, and no seam flushes the frame mid-frame (review-1 F3/F4/F5)

**Risk: high** — the frame's draw order on a target this host cannot look at, plus
the disposition of a High finding against the loop's own guard.

### The review this batch answers

`logs/ralph-pi/run-20261102-004416/review-1.md`, on `14cc4b4..1e2593c` plus the
uncommitted harness work. Six findings: **F1 High, F2 Medium, F3 Medium, F4 Low,
F5 Low, F6 Low**. Three are fixed here, three are recorded with evidence as
owner-gated or mechanically impossible for a batch. The reviewer also confirmed
the committed renderer independently (the depth rule re-derived from
`Renderer.cs:565,605-607`, the `C3D_DepthMap`/`C3D_DepthTest`/`C3D_FrameBufClear`
disassembly re-run on the linked archive, ten mutations of `pica_matrix` all
caught, the eye sign re-derived), which is the part of batch 29-30 this batch
does not have to re-litigate.

### F3 (Medium, confirmed, FIXED): the diagnostic triangle cost two depth writes and a draw per real draw

`diagnosticTriangle` is `true` in the shipping build and nothing ever cleared it,
and the triangle was drawn at the tail of **every** `drawRecorded`. Because the
triangle must not be depth-tested (it sits at clip `z = 0`, the far plane, which
is what the buffer was cleared to), it called `installDepthState({false,false})`
every draw — so the per-draw cache missed on every following draw and re-installed
the pass's state. Per eye, per frame, on the pinned scene's frame 1 (154 `Solid` +
1 `DoubleSided`, `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md`):

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `C3D_DepthTest` calls | ~310 (one per real draw + one per diagnostic) | **2** (the frame install, the diagnostic) |
| diagnostic draws | 155 | **1** |
| MVP uniform writes | one extra per draw — the diagnostic set `matrixIsFrame = false`, so the matrix cache was defeated every draw | only the frame's, per eye |
| BufInfo / TexEnv rebuilds | one per real draw | one per eye |

and the per-eye replay multiplied all of it by the eye count. The fix is a move,
not a new mechanism: `drawDiagnostic(r)` is called from the eye loop in
`mdk_render_end_frame`, immediately after that eye's `replayQueue`, so it runs
**once per eye** — inside the loop, not after it, or stereo would get a triangle in
one eye and a hole in the other.

Moving it also made it a better instrument, which is why this is not just a cost
cut:

* it now runs on a frame that queued **nothing**. Inside the per-draw path it could
  not — no draw, no diagnostic — and an empty frame is exactly where "is the frame
  and the program alive at all" is the only question left; such a frame showed
  nothing but the clear colour, i.e. the same picture as the failure it exists to
  distinguish.
* nothing real is drawn after it inside an eye, so the state it leaves behind (the
  context's single `BufInfo` and `TexEnv`, the identity uniform, the test off)
  cannot damage a draw of this frame. That hazard is not hypothetical: the vault's
  hardware-**confirmed** `30-architecture/patterns/c3d-interleaved-draw-leaves-vertex-uniforms-stale.md`
  is precisely an interleaved draw that switches vertex streams and leaves the
  **vertex uniforms** stale, with a later, unrelated draw landing off-screen while
  every state probe reads correct. Batch 28's defect in this same file was the
  mirror-image of it (the diagnostic drawn *before* the real draw replaced the
  context's `BufInfo` and the mesh read the triangle's 15 floats). The next
  `installEye` now cleans up after it, and `installEye` writes every uniform and
  every piece of fixed state anyway (AGENTS.md P2).

**Why not the reviewer's `__3DS_DEBUG__` gate.** Two reasons, both on record in
this repository. AGENTS.md §7/§10 keep this tree free of `#ifdef` forks (the
backend split is by file), and the vault's own
`30-architecture/patterns/build-the-off-switch-before-the-fix.md` — a confirmed
case where five instruments agreed and a runtime toggle settled it — says prefer a
**runtime** switch over a build flag, because a rebuild-per-arm tempts you to skip
the negative arm. `r->diagnosticTriangle` already *is* runtime state; what it lacks
is a way to flip it without a rebuild. That is now a named follow-up (an SD-file
switch next to `sdmc:/3ds/mdk/mdk.log`, `log_3ds.cpp:42-49`), not a compile-time
define. The triangle's geometry and position are deliberately unchanged: shrinking
it to keep the scene visible is a call for whoever first looks at a screen, and
this batch does not get to make a decision that only a screen can make.

### F4 (Low, confirmed, FIXED): a canvas/inset flush emitted the frame into a stale target and consumed it

`mdk_render_canvas_begin`, `mdk_render_begin_inset` and `mdk_render_end_inset`
still called `flushDraws`, which replays the queue and empties it. Since batch 30
the queue is replayed per eye at the frame end, so a mid-frame flush draws this
frame's records into **whatever target `installEye` last selected** — the previous
frame's last eye, or no target at all on frame 1 — and then leaves the eye loop an
empty queue. The reviewer's wording is the better one than `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md`
had used: not "it will appear in one eye only" but **the scene vanishes behind a
correct clear colour**. AGENTS.md P2 is the rule: a draw must follow the
`C3D_FrameDrawOn` of the target it lands in.

Nothing calls those seams on the 3DS (`grep` for `canvas_begin`/`begin_inset`
outside the backends is empty, and `mdk_render_canvas_quad` is a no-op on this
backend), which is the only reason this was Low and not Critical. The seams are now
documented no-ops, `flushDraws` is deleted, and `replayQueue`'s comment states the
contract: **the only replay point is `mdk_render_end_frame`, once per eye**. The
requirement for whoever lands the HUD is written into `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md`: a
canvas quad or an inset is a *record in the queue*, drawn inside the eye loop once
per eye with its own viewport — not a mid-frame flush.

### The pin: `PASS C3dFrame` (`tests/scripts/c3d_frame_test.sh`)

`renderer_c3d.cpp` includes `<3ds.h>` and cannot be compiled on a host, so — unlike

| `depth-state-single-writer` | a second `C3D_DepthTest` call site, i.e. a writer behind the cache's back |

and five mutation arms, each of which must turn a check red — because a gate whose

### B (High, confirmed, FIXED): `PASS C3dFrame` could be printed with the diagnostic outside the eye loop

The reviewer built two mutants and ran the gate. Reproduced here first, against
the shipped gate:

| mutant | shipped gate's verdict |
|---|---|
| `{ installEye; replayQueue; }` then `drawDiagnostic(r);` after the loop | all 5 checks **ok** |
| `drawDiagnostic(r);` **before** `replayQueue(r);` inside the loop | all 5 checks **ok** |

Both exited 1, but only because the arm `diagnostic-dropped-from-the-eye-loop`
replaces the literal two-line string `"        replayQueue(r);\n        drawDiagnostic(r);"`,
which the mutants no longer contain — so it printed "the mutation changed
nothing". The *check* `diagnostic-called-per-eye` asked only "exactly one call,
somewhere inside `mdk_render_end_frame`", which is true of both mutants. The
reviewer's failure scenario is the damaging part: a builder who reverts the
placement, sees that arm's "the mutation changed nothing", and retargets the arm
at the lone `drawDiagnostic(r);` line, then gets `PASS C3dFrame (5 checks, 5
arms adjudicated red)` over a frame with a triangle in one eye and a hole in the
other. That is a pass generator whose red was incidental.

Fixed by pinning the claimed shape instead of the call's existence. The gate now
brace-matches the per-eye loop out of `mdk_render_end_frame` and asserts:

* `diagnostic-called-in-the-eye-loop` — exactly one call site in the file **and
  it is inside the loop body**;
* `diagnostic-drawn-after-its-replay` — inside the loop, the replay's line index
  is strictly less than the diagnostic's (before it is batch 28's invisible
  geometry, where the mesh read the triangle's floats);
* `replay-only-at-frame-end` — the single replay is inside the loop, not merely
  inside the function.

Two new arms reproduce the reviewer's two mutants. Measured on the three
mutants, each now fails **on a check**, not on an arm mismatch:

```
mB1 (diag after the loop)   FAIL diagnostic-called-in-the-eye-loop: 1 call(s); inside the eye loop: no
                            FAIL diagnostic-drawn-after-its-replay: loop line 2 replays, loop line None draws
mB2 (diag before the replay) FAIL diagnostic-drawn-after-its-replay: loop line 3 replays, loop line 2 draws
```

and on the real source all 6 checks are ok and all 8 arms adjudicate red:
`PASS C3dFrame (6 checks, 8 arms adjudicated red)`.

Two bugs found in my own first version of the fix, both caught by the arms and
worth recording because they are the general failure:

1. `body()` no longer requires the `{` in its match, so it matched the forward
   declaration `static void drawDiagnostic(RendererC3D* r);` first and returned
   an unrelated block as the function body. The `{` is back in the pattern with a
   comment saying why.
2. The loop span was an offset **inside the function-body substring**, and the
   checks sliced the whole file with it, so every loop-relative check silently

### F1 (High, confirmed, FIXED): the emission set is now closed, not listed

Reproduced first: `mdk_render_canvas_quad` is a one-line no-op
(`renderer_c3d.cpp:1827`) and `hud_view.cpp:162,198,255` calls only that seam, while
the seam list named five functions and the forbidden pattern named only

inside `canvas_quad` was accepted green, and `docs/CONTINUATION.md` claimed the
opposite.

Three changes, because "the seams do not flush" was never the whole rule:

1. `canvas_quad` joined `SEAMS`, and the seam pattern is now **every emitter**:
   `flushDraws | replayQueue | drawRecorded | C3D_DrawArrays | C3D_DrawElements`.
2. New check `emission-sites-closed`: every `C3D_DrawArrays`/`C3D_DrawElements`
   call site in the file lies inside `drawRecorded` or `drawDiagnostic`.
3. New check `recorded-draws-only-from-the-replay`: every `drawRecorded` call site
   lies inside `replayQueue`.

(2) and (3) together are what makes *"the only emission point is the per-eye loop"*
a checked property instead of a reading of the file: a seam cannot draw, a new
function cannot draw, and the one function that draws records is reachable only from
the replay the loop calls.

second is the shape a HUD batch writes when it reads the contract as "do not flush"
rather than "the queue is the only way": it builds a `MeshDraw` and calls

### Three bugs in this batch's own first version, caught by its own arms

1. `calls()` builds its definition-skip out of the pattern it is given, so handing it
   the alternation `C3D_DrawArrays\s*\(|C3D_DrawElements\s*\(` made **every** line
   containing `C3D_DrawElements(` look like a definition and silently skip it — a
   check that could never see its own subject. Fixed by a separate `sites()` helper
   with no definition-skip, and the reason is in its docstring.
2. `install-after-its-replay` spliced the call back to the position it had just
   removed (inserting at the replay's start, not its end), so the "mutant" was the
   original file. The arm's own fail-closed rule — a mutation that changes nothing is
   a FAIL, never a skip — reported `only 15 of 16 arms adjudicated red`.
3. The first `install-hoisted-above-the-eye-loop` moved the call verbatim above the
   loop, which does not compile (`error: 'eye' was not declared in this scope`): an
   arm that cannot be shipped is not a defect. It now hoists a fixed-target call,
   which is both valid and the realistic tidy-up.

### What the review said, and what was checked first

Review-4's four actionable findings were all one gap: the gate pinned which
statements the per-eye loop **contains**, never that the loop **runs once per
eye** or that the queue **survives the run**. Each was reproduced before being

F2, F3 and F5 were confirmed exactly as written: green gate over a one-eye or a

### The fixes — eight checks, nine arms, nothing removed

| Finding | New check | What it refuses |
|---|---|---|
| F3 | `eye-loop-runs-every-pass` | any `break`/`continue`/`return` inside the loop body |
| F5 | `eye-loop-bound-is-the-eye-plan` | a bound that is not `…->eyes.passes` |
| F5 (sibling) | `eye-loop-starts-at-the-first-eye` | an initialiser other than `int eye = 0` |
| F2 | `frame-end-reset-after-the-eye-loop` | a reset inside `end_frame` at or before the loop's closing brace |
| F2 | `per-eye-functions-do-not-empty-the-queue` | a reset inside `replayQueue`/`drawRecorded`/`drawDiagnostic` |
| F2 (other half) | `queue-reset-happens-in-the-frame` | a frame that never clears the queue at all |

### Two places the reviewer's recommendation was refined rather than followed

* **F2 said "require exactly one reset site in the file."** That is not the
  invariant, and applying it would refuse the shipped source: `renderer_c3d.cpp`
  legitimately resets in **two** places, `mdk_render_begin_frame` (`:784`, the
  frame's eviction boundary, which `frameStartUse` and AGENTS.md P3 depend on)
  and after the eye loop in `mdk_render_end_frame` (`:858`). The check is
  therefore scoped to `end_frame` and phrased as a *position* ("no reset at or
  before the loop's closing brace"), not a count.
* **The reviewer's `m5_no_reset` mutant is deliberately NOT pinned.** Deleting
  only the end-of-frame reset is behaviourally equivalent here: draws cannot be
  added outside a frame (`mdk_render_draw_mesh` returns when `!inFrame`), and
  `begin_frame` clears the queue. A gate that refuses a non-defect is a false
  positive waiting to be weakened, so the arm instead removes **both** boundary
  resets, which is the real defect. This is said out loud because the mutant file
  is in the reviewer's set and a reader would otherwise expect it to be red.

**Prior-solution lookup.** Pi knowledge `mdk-sdl` (mode hybrid) returned the oracle's

(`FOOT1`-`FOOT4` on the run frames) and the `LAND` sound are not ported"), which is

vault was read directly (read-only) from `/mnt/nas/Vaults/port-docs`: no note mentions

harness-nondeterminism-forks-are-trajectory-not-rendering.md` is the same class of
problem as the feet drift this batch hit (a sim trajectory fork masquerading as a
rendering difference), and it is the reason the golden quantizes the feet instead of
chasing the pixels. Cognee MCP is not exposed in this Pi session and was not consulted.

### What landed

`Player` now owns the sounds C# `Kurt` makes from the state machine this port already
carries, and they are pinned. Oracle references, all in `src/Mdk.Game/Kurt/Kurt.cs`:

| Ported | Oracle | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Player::footstep` | `Kurt.Footstep` (Kurt.cs:716-731) | `LeftStep`/`RightStep` 0/13, `FireLeftStep`/`FireRightStep` 4/17, `_footstepPair` starting `true` and flipping only on the right foot |
| the previous/current frames in `Player::animate` | `Kurt.Animate`'s Run branch (Kurt.cs:692-705) | `Wrap((int)MathF.Floor(AnimationFrame), count)` before and after the advance; the **floor** is load-bearing because backing up runs the frame negative and `Wrap` maps it back |
| `playSound("LAND")` | `Kurt.UpdateState` (Kurt.cs:655) | on the Jump/RunJump/Fall/Chute → Land transition, before `SetState` |
| `playSound("CHUTEOUT")` | `Kurt.UpdateAir` (Kurt.cs:433) | where `ChuteOpen` becomes true |
| `Player::updateChuteSound` | `Kurt.UpdateChuteSound` (Kurt.cs:455-470) | `CHUTEON` with `Once` after `ChuteOpenFrames` (4), and the `Stop` + `CHUTEIN` when the chute closes; called where the C# calls it, i.e. **before** the Hang/HardLand branch, so a crashing Kurt's chute still closes |
| `Player::stopChuteSound` | `Kurt.StopChuteSound` (Kurt.cs:474) | on the death path; the ride, cutscene and ledge callers are not ported |

`Player::setMixer` mirrors C# `Kurt`'s constructor argument; a `Player` with no mixer
plays nothing, which is what both shipped frontends are today (the sample plane of
`AudioDevice.cs` is not ported, and the only mixer in a shipped build is
`ScriptRuntime`'s own, handed out `const`). That gap is recorded in `OPEN_ITEMS.md`
with the reason it is not this batch's to close. `RunFire`'s step frames are ported
with the rest of `Footstep` even though nothing writes `Firing` yet, so the firing
slice cannot quietly use the walking pair.

### The golden, and how it was derived

`tests/scripts/golden/L3_kurt_steps.txt` — 471 lines, the oracle probe's `kurt` mode
byte for byte. The probe (the scratch tree at `/tmp/mdk-pi/obj3`, rebuilt with
`/tmp/mdk-pi/build_probe.sh`) drives `kurt.Update(input, Viewer.Step)` for 470 steps
with `Input.Hold(Key.Forward/Back/Jump, …)` — the C#'s own test-input seam — from the
level's start, and prints state, feet, yaw, the three speeds, the animation frame, the
floor and chute flags, and the mixer's live voices in launch order. Reproduce with
`DOTNET_ROOT=/tmp/kilo/dotnet10 MDK_DATA_DIR=$PWD/MDK mdkprobe 3 470 1 kurt`; the C++
twin is `tests/scripts/build/tick1 dump kurt 3 470`.

Two things the probe needed that it did not have. `Kurt`'s third constructor argument is
the frame-count function, and the probe had `_ => 0`; `KurtSprite` cannot be built
headless (it needs a `Renderer`), so the probe reads `KurtSprite`'s own private
`Animations` table by reflection and the counts from `TRAVSPRT.BNI` — the two steps
`KurtSprite.FrameCount(state)` performs. `tick1` has the same table written out and
both sides print it in the header line (`counts=Still=10,…,Run=24,…`), so a table that
disagrees fails the golden loudly instead of drifting. `K_RUN` has 24 frames, which is
what makes `RightStep = 13` reachable at all. The mixer's voice list is private in C#
too, so the probe reads `_voices` by reflection; the C++ side prints the public
`SoundMixer::voices()`. Neither touches the oracle's source: the probe's `src/**.cs`
still differs from the read-only oracle only in the three known print-only files.

The schedule was chosen to cover every branch of the sound code, and it came out of
measuring the level rather than guessing it: the forward run walks Kurt off the start
pad, so the first `LAND` comes from a fall rather than a jump; the back-up phase runs
the animation frame negative (that is where `Wrap` and the floor of a negative frame
are the whole story); the second forward run crosses the step frames going the other
way, which is what produces `FOOT3` (the pair's other branch); and the jump is held
long enough to open the chute and released long enough to close it. The golden's
`voices=` sequence is `LAND`, `FOOT4`, `FOOT1`, `FOOT2`, `FOOT4`, `FOOT1`, `FOOT2`,
`FOOT3`, `CHUTEOUT`, `CHUTEON`, `CHUTEIN`, `LAND` — and because `CHUTEON` is `Stop`ped
before `CHUTEIN`, the column also pins that a stopped voice leaves the mixer's list.

### The feet drift, and the finding it exposed

At four decimals the feet did **not** match: 20 printed fields differed, growing to
1.34e-05 and no further. The cause is not the BSP and not the accumulator — it is
`Player::facing()`, which takes its sine and cosine from the trig LUT while C#
`Kurt.Facing` uses `MathF.Cos/Sin`, and `util/math_lut.h` documents the LUT's error as
4.76e-06 per period. `util/matrix.h`'s `create_from_axis_angle` already carries an
`@vfp-exempt R6` pin for exactly this reason, and Facing is gameplay: it decides where
every walk step lands, where the follow camera sits and where the velocity points.

Swapping the two calls for `cosf/sinf` makes the golden match at four decimals with no
other change, **and** moves the pinned frame closer to the oracle: `1.240 / 247 /
0.1819` → `1.095 / 247 / 0.1636`, measured against the same oracle pixels on
`DISPLAY=:99` with lavapipe. It is **not** landed, because it changes the picture and
`tests/frames/reference.sha256` is owner-protected — the `cpp=` baseline has to be
regenerated by the owner, and a batch may not do that to obtain a green frame gate. So
the golden prints the feet in 64ths of a unit (byte-exact, with ~1000x margin over the
drift), the finding is recorded in `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md` with its measurement and its
exact one-line shape, and the frame above is the unchanged one. This is the vault's
"trajectory, not rendering" fork, caught before it could be aimed at the renderer.

### What landed

This batch is test coverage, not a product-code change. It fixes review-7 F3's confirmed
finding that the comments claiming the hard-landing and death chute-sound behaviour were
not pinned: the reviewer removed `stopChuteSound()` from the death branch and moved

`tests/scripts/tick1.cpp`'s `dump kurt` scenario and the scratch C# probe's `kurt` mode

* steps 1-470 are batch 36's walk/run/back-up/jump schedule, unchanged;
* step 471 lifts Kurt 300 units above the start and zeroes his vertical speed, so the
  otherwise unreachable hard-landing speed can be produced;
* the jump at step 642 opens the chute at -182 u/s; its 3.9 u/s-per-step brake still
  leaves a -124 u/s landing at step 656, which enters `HardLand` and closes the chute;
* step 657 is the pin for the call order: the chute is closed but `CHUTEON` is still
  live, and only `updateChuteSound()` **before** the `HardLand` return can stop it and

  C# oracle's public kill seam (`Kurt.Combat.cs:169`); the landing at step 902 finds
  health zero on a floor and enters `Dead`;
* step 903 is the pin for the death path: `stopChuteSound()` removes `CHUTEON` **without**
  `CHUTEIN`, exactly as C# `Kurt.StopChuteSound` does.

### What landed

`golden/L3_kurt_lethal.txt` (201 lines, sha256 `0723fd82…`) is a **second scripted Kurt

line — and step 183 is the landing.

What that reaches is the C#'s `HardLanding` early return, which no previous run could:

```csharp
if (Health > 0) Damage(HardLandingDamage);
KnockDamage = 0f;
if (Health == 0 || Current is State.Dead or State.Knocked or State.GetUp) return;   // Kurt.cs:584
StopFiring(); ChuteOpen = false; SetState(State.HardLand);
```

The 950-step schedule visits a hard landing at full health and a death on a *soft*
landing, and Kurt only dies once, so the two can never share a run. The new golden
pins the third case: a Kurt already at 0 who arrives at -194 u/s does **not** enter
`K_CRASHL`, does **not** have his chute closed for him, and does not take the 10
points again — the oracle prints `s=183 state=Dead … vert=0.0000 floor=1 chute=0
hp=0`, and the death frame advances from 184 on.

Harness, both sides, same literal: `tick1 dump kurtlethal <level> <steps>`
(`dumpKurt(…, bool lethal)`) and the probe's `kurtlethal` mode. The existing
schedule is untouched — its phases are now guarded on `!lethal` — and the probe's
`kurt` mode still reproduces `L3_kurt_steps.txt` byte for byte, so the 950-step pin
did not move.

Oracle reference: `Kurt.cs:576-590` (`HardLanding`), `Kurt.cs:560-572` (`Land`),
`Kurt.Combat.cs:135-150` (`Damage`, `Health = Math.Max(Health - damage, 0)`),
`Kurt.Combat.cs:373-378` (`Health == 0 && OnFloor → State.Dead`).

next slice, not a line in this one, because unifying them is a state-model change and
no existing golden can pin the bridge.

`KurtSprite` headlessly: the C# constructor needs the sealed Vulkan `Renderer`, and
`KurtSprite::load` refuses a null one even though the decode only copies palette
indices. The two candidate seams are written out in `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md`.

## Iteration 68 — batch 40: Kurt has one health again, pinned from both sides of the class split (review-10 F4/F5 fixed; F1/F2/F3/F6 owner-gated)

### What landed

**Priority item 6a: the two healths are one.** The C# `Kurt` is one class with one
`Health` (`Kurt.Combat.cs:76`): `Damage` writes it, `Hurt` reaches it from
`hurt_kurt` (opcode 109), and the same field is what
`Health == 0 && OnFloor → State.Dead` reads and what the HUD draws. This port splits
the class into `mdk::Player` (movement) and `mdk::Kurt` (combat) and had **two**
healths with nothing between them, so a script that hurt Kurt to zero neither moved
the HUD nor killed him. Now:

| change | effect |
|---|---|
| `Player::health` (field) → `Player::combat_` (`Kurt` member) + `health()` | the health lives in the combat half and nowhere else |
| `Kurt::setHealth` / `Kurt::damageHealth` | `Player::setHealth`/`damage` are the C#'s `SetHealth` and the `Health` line of `Damage`, on the one field |
| `ScriptRuntime::kurt()` → `player_->combat()` when a Player is bound | the runtime hands out the entity's own object, as C# `Viewer`'s single `Kurt` is handed in (`ScriptRuntime.cs:168`); no copy |
| `ScriptRuntime`'s `const Player*` → `Player*` | the runtime borrows the whole entity, not a read-only view (source-compatible at every call site) |
| `mdk_linux/src/main.cpp:633` | the HUD reads `player.health()`, i.e. the field opcode 241 reads |

A runtime built with **no** Player (the harnesses that pass `nullptr`, as the ctor
documents) falls back to the runtime's own `unboundKurt_`, renamed from `kurt_` to say
what it is: the combat state of a world with no Kurt entity, with no second copy of
anything. The shipped frontend binds its Player, so in the shipped unit there is one
health, full stop.

### The pin, and what it kills

`tests/scripts/golden/L3_kurt_hurt.txt` — **221 lines, sha256 `35d78b3d…`**, the C#
oracle probe's new `hurt` mode, byte-identical to `tick1 dump hurt 3 220`. It steps the
`ScriptRuntime` and the same `Kurt` object together in the frontend's order (Kurt, then
the scripts — `Viewer.cs:505-535`), and prints **`hp=`** (the entity's health: what the
death transition and the HUD read) and **`vmhp=`** (what the VM reads through
`ScriptRuntime::kurt()`). In the oracle those are one property and cannot disagree,
which is the entire content of the golden.

The scenario hurts him **in mid-air**, on purpose: on a floor any hurt of ≥5 knocks the
oracle's Kurt down (`UpdateKnockDamage`, `KnockDamage >= 5` while `OnFloor`) and the
port has no knock-down state machine, so a ground hurt would compare an oracle in
`K_BANG` against a port standing still. The oracle itself declines to knock him unless
it finds a floor within 13 units below, so the run lifts him 300 units and hurts him at
steps 20/40/60/80 (10/25/30/35 → health 100→90→65→35→0) and again at 200, on the corpse
(`Hurt`'s `Health == 0` early return). Step 183 is the landing: `state=Dead`, the same
lethal hard landing batch 39 pinned.

Mutants built and run:

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| `ScriptRuntime::kurt()` returns its own copy (the pre-fix state) | **FAILS** at the first hurt — `s=20 hp=100 vmhp=90` — and at the landing, `s=183 state=HardLand hp=90` where the oracle is `Dead` |
| (kept) `Player::damage` floors at 0 | unchanged, as batch 39 proved |

### What landed

**Review-11 R11-3 (High): the state half of the class split, so `Kurt::hurt`'s guard
reads the state the machine is in.** The C# `Kurt` is one object: `Current` is a field
of it (`Kurt.cs:104`) and `Hurt` reads that same field
(`Kurt.Combat.cs:120`: `if (Invulnerable > 0f || Current is State.Dead or State.Knocked
or State.GetUp or State.HardLand) { KnockDamage = 0f; return; }`). This port splits the
class and had the state in `mdk::Player::_state` while `mdk::Kurt::state_` — the copy
`hurt()` reads — had **no writer at all**, so the guard could never fire.

| change | effect |
|---|---|
| `Kurt::setState(State)` added; `Kurt::state_` documented as the one state | the combat half owns the state, as the C#'s one object does |
| `Player::_state` **deleted**; `Player::state()` → `combat_.state()` | there is no second copy to drift; `Player::setState` is the only writer, through `combat_.setState` |
| `player.cpp`: 20 reads of `_state` → `state()` | mechanical, no value moved (all four Kurt goldens pass unchanged) |

This is deliberately the same shape batch 40 gave the health, for the same reason: a
copy on either side of the split is a copy the other half never sees. The alternative
the reviewer also offered — have `Player::setState` mirror into a second field — was
rejected because it re-introduces exactly the duplication batch 40 removed.

The reviewer's second observation, that a hurt taking health to zero inside the crash
window would defer the death (because `Player::update` returns through `updateSpecial`
while the state is `HardLand`), is closed by the same change: with the guard live, no
hurt reaches the health in that window at all, so there is no deferred death to defer.

**Review-11 R11-4 (Low): the `L3_kurt_hurt` PASS message over-claimed.** It said the
fixture shows hurt_kurt "takes Kurt to Dead on the landing". The step that makes him
Dead is the health-zero-on-a-floor transition, which `L3_kurt_lethal` pins on its own;
what this fixture discriminates is `hp == vmhp`. The message now says that, and the
comment above the block says what the run does *not* pin.

**Review-11 R11-5 (Low): `Kurt::slots_` was default-initialised, not
value-initialised.** Now `Slot slots_[kMaxSlots]{};`, matching `ammo_[]`. The harnesses
copy `Player` (and therefore `Kurt`) by value, so an indeterminate subarray is a read of
uninitialised memory even with `slotCount_ == 0` gating every reader.

### The pin, and what it kills

`tests/scripts/golden/L3_kurt_hurtland.txt` — **341 lines, sha256 `9e1b4832…`**, the C#
oracle probe's new `hurtland` mode (`mdkprobe 3 340 1 hurtland`), byte-identical to
`tick1 dump hurtland 3 340`. Same world as the hurt golden (reachable arenas, the

same step order (Kurt, then the scripts). The schedule lifts him 300 units at step 1, so
the landing at **step 183** is a hard one (−194 u/s) and K_CRASHL runs 26 frames at 4 per
second = **104 steps, 183..286**; then:

| step | state | oracle | what a wrong port prints |
|---|---|---|---|
| 220 (inside the window) | `HardLand` | hurt of 10 **refused**, `hp=90` | `hp=80` — the guard read a state nothing wrote |
| 300 (after the window) | `Still` | hurt of 4 taken, `hp=86` | `hp=90` — the guard never releases |

The second damage is **4, not 5**, on purpose: on a floor a hurt of ≥5 knocks the oracle
down (`UpdateKnockDamage`, `KnockDamage >= 5` while `OnFloor`) and the knock-down machine
is not ported, so the release arm has to be provable without dragging in a subsystem
neither side has. `KnockDamage` is 0 at step 300 because the C#'s `HardLanding` zeroes it
after the damage (`Kurt.cs:584`), which the port also does.

Mutants built and run (library files swapped to HEAD's, the new test kept):

## Iteration 70 — batch 42: the knock counter declines, and a hard landing zeroes it (review-12 A/C/D/E fixed; B owner-gated)

**Prior-solution lookup (all three sources, before implementing).** *Pi knowledge
(`mdk-sdl` KB, `knowledge_search`, mode `hybrid`)*: returned `Kurt.Combat.cs`'s
`UpdateKnockDamage` and its constant block, `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md`'s knock-down entry, and
`mdk_core/src/game/kurt.cpp`'s `hurt()` — i.e. the KB already carried this subsystem's
open item and pointed at the same two rules this batch landed; treated as a lead and
verified against the oracle. *Obsidian*: no MCP server is exposed in this Pi session, so
the vault was read directly (read-only) from `/mnt/nas/Vaults/port-docs`; a recursive grep
for `knockdown|knock_down|K_BANG` found **nothing** — no prior note on this subsystem.
*Cognee MCP*: **not available** — no Cognee tool is exposed in this session, so the
knowledge graph was **not** consulted; recorded rather than implied.

### What landed, and the oracle line behind it

`golden/L3_kurt_hurt.txt` and `golden/L3_kurt_hurtland.txt` both keep their hurts in the
air, and both say why: on a floor a hurt of 5 or more knocks the oracle down, and the
knock-down state machine is not ported. That deferral had quietly taken two more rules
with it, and review-12 A found the second one by reading the field's writers:

1. **The counter's decline** — `Kurt.UpdateKnockDamage`'s tail (`Kurt.Combat.cs:230-231`)
   is `KnockDamage = Math.Clamp(KnockDamage, 0f, KnockdownDamage)` and then
   `KnockDamage = MathF.Max(KnockDamage - KnockdownDrain * delta, 0f)`. Ported as
   `Kurt::declineKnockDamage`, called from `Player::update` at the C#'s own call site
   (`Kurt.cs:176`: after the ride and noclip returns, before `UpdateChuteSound` and
   before the `Hang`/`HardLand` branch, so a crashing Kurt's counter declines too).
2. **The hard landing's reset** — `Kurt.HardLanding` writes `KnockDamage = 0f`
   unconditionally at `Kurt.cs:583`, *between* the damage call and the
   `Health == 0 || Current is Dead|Knocked|GetUp` guard. The port wrote nothing, so a
   counter a script raised with `set_hurt_flash` (opcode 240) or a hurt taken in the air
   survived a landing the oracle clears. Ported as `combat_.setKnockDamage(0.0f)` in
   `Player::land`, at that position.

That second one is why this batch is not merely cosmetic: the moment the knock-down
trigger exists, a counter that survives a hard landing knocks Kurt down on the step
*after* every hard landing. It is also what made the previous batch's record wrong — see
the disposition of review-12 A below.

The **trigger half** of `UpdateKnockDamage` is deliberately NOT ported, and this batch
replaced a vague deferral with the three named things it actually needs
(`docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md`): `ArenaSpace::floor` — the C# probe is `ArenaSpace.Floor(from, to,
out point)` (`ArenaSpace.cs:191`), which searches the arenas around **both** ends and
keeps the **nearest** crossing, while the port's `floorCrossing` is the C#'s *other* probe
`FloorCrossing` (`ArenaSpace.Probes.cs:19`), Kurt's arenas around `from` only and the
**first** hit; the `Knocked`/`GetUp` arms of `Kurt.UpdateCombatState`
(`Kurt.Combat.cs:379-399`), without which entering `Knocked` strands Kurt in a state
nothing animates and nothing exits; and the invulnerability decay `Invulnerable =
MathF.Max(Invulnerable - delta, 0f)` (`Kurt.cs:139`), which the port does not run at all,
so opcode 244's invulnerability currently lasts forever. `KnockDown`'s `StopFiring()`
stays inert with the firing slice.

### The pin, and the three mutants

`tests/scripts/golden/L3_kurt_knock.txt` — **341 lines, sha256 `5c2c3091…`**, the oracle
probe's new `knock` mode (`mdkprobe 3 340 1 knock`), byte-identical to
`tick1 dump knock 3 340`. It lifts Kurt 300 units (the hard landing's own fixture, so the
landing is step 183 and K_CRASHL runs to 286) and prints `knock=` — the oracle's own
`Kurt.KnockDamage` — every step:

| step | oracle | what it pins |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | `hp=75 knock=25.0000` | `hurt_kurt` 25 high in the air, where the knock-down probe cannot reach a floor |
| 21 | `knock=4.9667` | the **clamp** to `KnockdownDamage` and the **drain** on the same step |
| 175→182 | `4.0000 → 3.7667` | the drain continuing, under the threshold so no knock-down |
| 183 | `state=HardLand hp=61 knock=0.0000` | the hard landing's **reset** |
| 300→304 | `3.0000 → 2.8667` | the drain on the floor, after the K_CRASHL window |

The probe was re-verified against a committed golden before use: `mdkprobe 3 220 1 hurt`
is byte-identical to `golden/L3_kurt_hurt.txt`. Mutants built and run (each rebuilt

`tests/scripts/vm_tests.cpp` gained three cases in `testKurtAndScreenWrites`, for the

## Iteration 71 — batch 43: Kurt's invulnerability is a timer again, not a switch (review-13 had no Critical/High; F3 fixed, F2 accepted, F1 owner-owned)

**Prior-solution lookup (all three sources, before implementing).** *Pi knowledge
(`mdk-sdl` KB, `knowledge_search`, mode `hybrid`, query "Kurt invulnerability decay
set_global_573bd4 opcode 244 never clears")*: result [1] was `mdk_core/src/game/kurt.h`'s
own `setInvulnerable` and result [5] was `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md`'s "The invulnerability decay"
entry — the KB already carried this exact open item, so the lookup confirmed the slice rather
than discovering it; verified against the oracle before writing anything. *Obsidian*: no MCP
server is exposed in this Pi session, so the vault was read directly (read-only) from
`/mnt/nas/Vaults/port-docs`; a recursive grep for `invulnerab` and for `573bd4|KnockdownInvulnerability`
found **nothing** — no prior note on this field. *Cognee MCP*: **not available** — no Cognee
tool is exposed in this session, so the knowledge graph was **not** consulted; recorded rather
than implied.

### What landed, and the oracle line behind it

`Kurt.Update`'s second statement is `Invulnerable = MathF.Max(Invulnerable - delta, 0f)`
(`src/Mdk.Game/Kurt/Kurt.cs:139`), immediately after the mouse-turn reset and **ahead of the
`Frozen` return (`:141`) and the `Current == State.Dead` return (`:152`)**. The field it writes
(`Kurt.Combat.cs:82`, `public float Invulnerable`, the original's 0x573bd4) has three readers:
`Hurt`'s guard (`Kurt.Combat.cs:125`, `Invulnerable > 0f` → no damage, and `KnockDamage = 0f`),
opcode 240 (`ScriptVm.cs:1590`, which refuses to raise the knock-down counter while
invulnerable), and opcode 244 itself (`ScriptVm.cs:1598`, whose accumulate arm adds to it).

The port had the field, opcode 244, and both readers — and no decay. So opcode 244, the only
writer this port has, was not a timer but a **switch**: the first script that set it made Kurt
immune to `hurt_kurt` and to the knock counter for the rest of the level, and every gate stayed
green because opcode 244 fires in none of levels 3-8. That is the same shape as batch 40's two
healths and batch 41's unwritten state: a field with a reader and no writer, invisible to a
golden that never sets it.

`Kurt::declineInvulnerability(delta)` is that line, and `Player::update` calls it at the C#'s
own position — the first statement, before `_chuteClosing = false` and before `if (dead)`, so a
dead Kurt's timer runs down too, and so it stays above the `Frozen`/noclip/`Ride` early returns
when those land (review-13's open question, which this batch answers for this field: the decay
is above them in the C#, so it must not move with them). `kurt.h` carries why the position is
load-bearing, and `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md`'s invulnerability item is closed, with the part of it
that is *not* closed named: `FadeFlashes` (`Kurt.Combat.cs:203`) is still unported, so nothing
fades `hurtFlash_` or `whiteFlash_`.

### The pin, and the three mutants

`tests/scripts/golden/L3_kurt_invuln.txt` — 341 lines, sha256 `fb00137b09cacca4…`, the oracle
probe's new `invuln` mode (`/tmp/mdk-pi/obj3/Probe`, rebuilt with `/tmp/mdk-pi/build_probe.sh`,
run as `mdkprobe 3 340 1 invuln`), byte-identical to `tick1 dump invuln 3 340`. Before
generating it the probe's `src/Mdk.Game/Kurt/Kurt.cs` and `Kurt.Combat.cs` were re-verified
byte-identical to the repository's read-only oracle (`59ea74c4…`, `19f8c7de…`), and the probe's
existing `knock` mode was re-run and re-diffed against `golden/L3_kurt_knock.txt` (identical),
so the fixture is oracle output and not the port's.

The schedule prints `invuln=` and `knock=` every step and prints itself in the header line:

| step | event | what it pins |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | `Invulnerable = 3` (opcode 244's set arm) | the value a knock-down would have set (`KnockdownInvulnerability`, `Kurt.Combat.cs:34`) |
| 40 | hurt 4 | refused: `hp=100` while `invuln=2.6667`, and the guard zeroes `knock` |
| 199→200 | — | `0.0167 → 0.0000`: the floor at zero, on the step it lands |
| 210 | hurt 4 | accepted: `hp=96` — the guard released because the timer expired |
| 280 | hurt 3 | accepted: `hp=93`, `knock=4.6667`, still under `KnockdownDamage` |
| 300→301 | `SetHealth(0)` | the death transition on the floor, `state=Dead` |
| 305→340 | `Invulnerable = 2` | `2.0000 → 1.4167` **on a corpse**: the decay is above the `dead` return |

Two design constraints, both learned by running the oracle rather than guessed. Nothing is
**lifted**: the HardLand state is the *other* arm of `Hurt`'s guard, and a lift would have made
every refused hurt ambiguous about which arm refused it. And the second accepted hurt sits at
step **280**, not 260: the first draft used 260, the oracle entered `State.Knocked` at 261 (the
counter was at 2.33, +3 crossed `KnockdownDamage`, and on a floor the trigger needs no floor
probe), and the port could not follow — the first version of this fixture therefore diffed for
exactly the reason the fixture exists to avoid. At 280 the counter has drained to 1.6667 and
4.6667 stays under the threshold.

Three mutants, built and run against the golden:

| mutant | first difference |
|---|---|
| no `declineInvulnerability` call at all | `s=21 invuln=3.0000` (oracle `2.9833`) |
| `invulnerable_ -= delta`, no floor at zero | `s=1 invuln=-0.0167` (oracle `0.0000`) |
| the call moved below `if (dead) return` | `s=306 invuln=2.0000` (oracle `1.9833`) |

`vm_tests` gains three cases for what the fixture cannot reach: the timer must not go negative
and must stay at zero once there; opcode 244's **accumulate** arm must add to a floored timer
(1.5 s after a drained timer is 1.5 s, not "1.5 s minus the overshoot", which is what a
negative timer would give); and the property the whole slice is about — `hurt()` refuses at
0.5 s and at 29/60 s and lands for 10 the step the timer reads 0.0000.

### What landed, and the oracle lines behind it

Four C# rules, all of them the ones every earlier hurt golden deliberately stepped around by
keeping its damage under `KnockdownDamage`:

1. **`ArenaSpace::floor`** is `ArenaSpace.Floor(from, to, out point)` (`ArenaSpace.cs:191`,
   the original's 0x421708): the arenas around **both** ends (`AddAt(from)` *and* `AddAt(to)`),
   the crossing **nearest `from`** by `Vector3.DistanceSquared`, and `point` initialised to
   `to`. It is a different probe from the port's existing `floorCrossing`, which is the C#'s
   `FloorCrossing` (`ArenaSpace.Probes.cs:19`): Kurt's arenas around `from` only — the pinned
   solid ones when there are any — and the **first** hit in arena order. Both header and
   comment say so, because writing them as one function is the mistake the pair invites.
2. **`Kurt::knocked()`** is `Kurt.Knocked` (`Kurt.Combat.cs:105`, `Current is Knocked or
   GetUp`), the guard the trigger needs so a Kurt already down is not knocked down again.
3. **`Player::knockDown`** is `Kurt.KnockDown` (`Kurt.Combat.cs:173`, state 901): counter
   spent, `Invulnerable = KnockdownInvulnerability`, push added, chute closed, `SetState
   (Knocked)`. Its `StopFiring()` is inert for the reason `Player::land` already records for
   the C#'s own call to it — nothing in this port fires.
4. **`Player::updateKnockDamage`** is `Kurt.UpdateKnockDamage` (`Kurt.Combat.cs:214`) whole,
   at the C#'s call site (`Kurt.cs:176`): the three guards (`Health > 0`, `KnockDamage >= 5`,
   `!Knocked`), then on a floor — or in the air when the 13-unit probe finds one, slamming him
   to `min(VerticalSpeed, -64)` — `KnockDown(Vector2.Zero)`; otherwise the decline tail that
   batch 42 ported. `Kurt::declineKnockDamage` is now what the C#'s tail is, and its comment
   no longer claims the trigger is unported.
5. **The `Knocked`/`GetUp` arms of `Player::updateState`** are `Kurt.UpdateCombatState`
   (`Kurt.Combat.cs:379-399`): `K_BANG` for `frameCount(Knocked)` frames, then the push
   cleared at the flip, `K_BFLIP` for `frameCount(GetUp)`, then `Still` — and the GetUp arm
   returns *false*, so the ordinary state selection and `Animate` run on the very step he
   stands up.
6. **The walk suppression** (`Kurt.cs:213-217`): thrown, knocked down or getting up, the walk
   *input* is zeroed (not the speed, so friction still carries him down to a stop) and the
   zeroed values are what reach `updateState`.

### The pins, and the six mutants

`tests/scripts/golden/L3_kurt_knockdown.txt` — 341 lines, sha256 `7e1862ea…`, the oracle
probe's new `knockdown` mode, byte-identical to `tick1 dump knockdown 3 340`. Before
generating it the probe was rebuilt (`/tmp/mdk-pi/build_probe.sh`) and its existing `invuln`,
`knock` and `hurt` modes were re-run and re-diffed against their committed goldens (all
identical), so the fixture is oracle output and not the port's.

| step | event | what it pins |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | hurt 5 on the start pad | `knock=5.0000` — the threshold, on a floor, with no floor probe needed |
| 21 | — | `state=Knocked invuln=3.0000 knock=0.0000 frame=0.5000`: KnockDown's three writes, on the step the trigger fires |
| 25..60 | forward held | `feet64` does not move: the walk input is dead while he is down |
| 30 | opcode-244 write of **0** | the timer is out of the way, so the next refusal can only be the state |
| 40 | hurt 4 | `hp=95`: refused by `hurt()`'s **Knocked** arm — the arm batch 41 named unreachable |
| 70 / 124 | — | `K_BANG` (25 frames) flips to `K_BFLIP` (27) and back to `Still`, `frame=` every step |
| 150 | lifted 6 units | airborne, `floor=0` |
| 156→157 | hurt 5 in the air | `vert=-65.0665` and `state=Knocked`: the 13-unit probe found the pad and the slam fired |

`tests/scripts/golden/L3_floor_probes.txt` — 49 lines, sha256 `a9e38021…`, the new `floor`
probe mode: `floor` and `floorCrossing` printed side by side over three segments (a long one
through the arena and 20 past its floor, the knock-down's own 13-unit shape, and the same
segment reversed) through each of level 3's 16 reachable arenas. They agree on 46 of 48 and
**part company on two** — the long segments through `HMO_9` and `CHMO_8`, where the nearest
crossing is `-286.0000` and the first crossing is `-326.6710` / `-326.5152`. That is the
nearest-vs-first rule separated on real geometry; the both-ends rule is exercised by the same
golden but no level-3 segment separates it from a `from`-only search, and that is stated here
rather than left for a reviewer to find.

Six mutants, all built and run:

| mutant | first difference |
|---|---|
| no trigger (batch 43's shape) | `s=21 state=Still … knock=4.9667` |
| no airborne arm | `s=157 state=Still … vert=-8.5327` |
| no slam | `s=157 vert=-8.5327` with `state=Knocked` |
| `KnockDown` does not spend the counter | `s=21 knock=5.0000` |
| no `Knocked`/`GetUp` arms | `s=21 state=Still` (the ordinary selection resets him) |
| no walk suppression | `s=25 feet64=-248,-11,12246` — he walks while flat on his back |

Three `vm_tests` cases cover what a schedule cannot reach: `KnockDownSpendsTheCounterAnd
OpensTheTimer` (the `!Knocked` guard, the timer declining rather than re-opening, `hurt()`
refusing for the state with the timer at zero, and a Player with **no arena space** finding no
floor to be slammed to), `AirborneKnockDownSlamsToTheFloorTheProbeReaches` (the floor found
first, then the slam asserted at `<= -64`), and `FloorProbeAnswersWhatTheTriggerAsks` (the
query finds a floor below, and on an empty space says no and leaves the out point at the
segment's own end — the C#'s `point = to`).

**What the goldens still cannot pin, named rather than left implicit.** The flip's leftover

exactly and the leftover is always `0.0000` (both flips in the golden read `frame=0.0000`).

the only caller the port has passes `Vector2.Zero` — `push_kurt` (opcode 248) is deferred with
cause — and therefore the push-clearing at the flip; and `ChuteOpen = false` inside `KnockDown`,
because nothing opens the chute while he is on the floor.

### What landed: the two flash fields become live state

`docs/CONTINUATION.md`'s "NEXT, same family" named this: nothing faded `hurtFlash_` or
`whiteFlash_`, so opcode 215's screen flash and `damage()`'s red flash stayed up forever, and
the death transition's `HurtFlash = 0` and `UpdateDeath`'s skull rise were the other half of
the same field. One subsystem slice, five files:

* **`Kurt::fadeFlashes`** (`Kurt.Combat.cs:203-206`, both lines verbatim) — both flashes fall
  by `kFlashFade` (4 per tick = 120/s) and floor at zero. `Player::update` calls it where
  `Kurt.Update` does (`Kurt.cs:159`): after the Frozen return (unported, and the note says it
  must fade on its own branch when it lands) and after the Dead return, so a corpse fades
  nothing — which is why a white flash that was up when Kurt died stays up for the whole death
  beat, the oracle's behaviour, now printed by the golden instead of assumed.
* **The death transition zeroes the flash** (`Kurt.Combat.cs:375`). `Player::updateState`'s
  death arm now calls `combat_.setHurtFlash(0.0f)`; the port splits the class, so the movement
  half needs the write the C# does through a private setter. The comment that deliberately left
  it out ("nothing fades it in this port yet") is gone, because that reason expired with this
  batch.
* **`Kurt::fadeSkullIn` + `skullFinished`** (`Kurt.Combat.cs:238, 250-253`) — `Player::updateDeath`
  returns before anything else once `hurtFlash_ > kSkullEnd`, and otherwise rises it by
  `kSkullFade` (60/s) and reports the step that passes the end. That step is the C#'s
  `Died?.Invoke()`, which §10 cannot spell as a delegate: it is a latch, `Player::died()`, set
  once and cleared by `setState` when Kurt leaves `Dead` (the C#'s `Revive` is the writer that
  would do it and is not ported), so it fires once per death exactly as the event does.
* **`Player::damage` is the C#'s `Damage` whole.** It used to call `Kurt::damageHealth`, the
  `Health` line alone, because the two terms it left out were inert while nothing faded the
  flash. `Kurt::damage` is now public (the C#'s `HardLanding` calls `Damage` directly,
  `Kurt.cs:580`, and the hard landing lives on Player here) and `damageHealth` is deleted — one
  implementation per behaviour. The slam now raises the red flash to its 180 clamp and adds to
  the knock counter, which `Player::land` zeroes two lines later exactly as `Kurt.cs:583` does.
  What is still left out is `Scaled(damage, Difficulty)`, inert because `difficulty_` has no
  writer, and the note at `land()` now says that instead of the expired one.
* **The Linux frontend stops faking the skull.** It had its own `kSkullFadePerSecond`,
  `kSkullEnd`, `kRespawnDelay` and `deathTimer`, and passed `deathTimer * 60` as the HUD's
  `hurtFlash`. All four are deleted: `state.hurtFlash` and `state.whiteFlash` now come off
  `player.combat()` the way `Viewer.HudStateOf` passes `kurt.HurtFlash`/`kurt.WhiteFlash`
  (`Viewer.cs:913`), and the respawn triggers on `player.died()` instead of a wall-clock timer,
  so the skull takes 255 steps to reach SkullEnd and Died fires on the next step that passes it
  (256 rising steps total); a stalled or faster-than-real-time frame cannot stretch it. The frontend's comment claimed a second divergence — "the C# beat
  can be SHORTER when HurtFlash is already partway up when Kurt dies" — which was never true:
  the death transition zeroes the flash, so the fade always starts from zero. Corrected.

### What landed

Opcode 248 had a C# implementation and was deferred only because the knockdown push had no live writer. `ScriptRuntime::pushKurt` now takes the decoded complete operand list and mirrors `ScriptRuntime.PushKurt` (`src/Mdk.Game/Scripts/ScriptRuntime.cs:2824-2852`): it refuses Kurt when already Knocked/GetUp or dead, mode 0 uses the oracle's intentionally asymmetric object-yaw formula and lift at args[3], nonzero mode normalizes C# runtime `KurtPosition - object.Position` (not live Player feet), uses the +X fallback for zero distance, and reads lift at args[2]. It passes the vector through `Player::knockDown(push)` before adding vertical speed, as C# `KnockDown` and `AddVerticalSpeed` do. VM opcode dispatch passes its entire decoded list.

### The NaN reachability argument (F7's open question, answered)

`MdkObject::speed` has exactly four kinds of writer in the port: `0.0f` (stop, stuck, arrival), the clamps themselves, opcode 53 `set_speed` (`script_vm.cpp:1058`, `obj->speed = value(obj, op(ins, 0))`), and `max_speed`/`acceleration`/`deceleration` from opcodes 50/51/52. `value()` returns either a bytecode literal or a script variable, and the VM's only variable arithmetic is `vars[i] = literal`, `vars[i] += literal` and `vars[i] += literal × Dt` (`script_vm.cpp:1082, 1094, 1106`) — no division, no indeterminate form. So a NaN speed requires a NaN literal in the shipped bytecode, and none is known. The test therefore pins the **semantics at the site**, exactly as `testRaiseShakeKeepsTheTickMaximum` already does for opcode 135, and is not claimed to be a reachable scenario.

Deferred with cause, not swept in: the remaining `fmaxf`/`fminf` sites in this file — the friction factor (`:815`, the C#'s `MathF.Max` at `ObjectMotion.cs:1066`), the gun-aim cone (`:1313`), the sweep-box span (`:1969-1970`) and the minimum height (`:3016`, the C#'s `MathF.Max` at `:1138`). NaN is equally unreachable at each, they belong to other subsystems (friction, gun aim, the BSP sweep, the camera), and each would want its own pin rather than riding in on a movement batch.

### Every expected value was derived from the oracle first

The float32 model of the C# expressions (`/tmp/mdk-pi/b49/`: `struct`-rounded `atan2`/`cos`/`sin`, `WrapAngle`, the gain's left-to-right multiply order) produced these numbers before the port was run against them, and the port matched on the first run, unedited.

| the left follower's first tick | heading `atan2(45,4) = 84.9204°` → clamp `+6`; `(cos 6, sin 6) × 50 / 30` → `(1.6575366, -39.8257866)`, `z = 0.0333333` | same |

### F2 (Medium) — confirmed, fixed, and pinned in both directions

The reviewer's claim: the batch-50 arrival test uses a **Walk** arrival, where `Walk`'s own early
`return` preempts the guard, so deleting the guard alone keeps every test green; the guard is
load-bearing on the **Fly** arrival. Checked against the oracle line by line:

| Oracle | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ObjectMotion.cs:354-358` | `if (obj.MoveCommand != 0) { DetectStuck(...); HandleStuck(...); }` — the guard exists |
| `Stop` `:792-797` | `MoveCommand = 0; Speed = 0; ContactFlags &= ~ContactStuck;` — **`StuckCount` is not touched** |
| `Walk` `:807-813` | on the final leg inside `Arrived` (5): `Stop(obj); return;` — Walk leaves the *method*, so the switch never reaches the guard |
| `Fly` `:848-860` | on arrival `Stop(obj);` and then `return;` **to the switch**, with `MoveCommand` already 0 — the guard is what skips the two calls |
| `DetectStuck` `:679-684` | `if (!collided \|\| Speed <= StuckSpeed(2)) { ResetStuck(obj); return; }` |
| `ResetStuck` `:703-708` | `StuckCount = 0` — so without the guard a fly arrival zeroes the count |
| `ScriptVm.cs:1243` (opcode 231) | branches on `MoveCommand == 0 && StuckCount != 0` — the direction is script-visible |

So the finding holds, and the fix is the pose the reviewer described. `testArrivalKeepsTheStuckCountTheOracleKeeps`
now runs three poses:

1. **Walk arrival** (unchanged): gravity flag, command 43, `waypoint == move_destination == (2,0,0)`
   (Manhattan 2 < `Arrived` 5, final) → `Stop`, `stuck_count` survives at 2.
2. **Fly arrival** (new, the one the guard decides): no gravity flag, command 78,
   `waypoint == move_destination == (2,0,0)` — Manhattan 2 is *not* `> TurnFrom` (3) so the turn is
   skipped, `horizontal 2 < ArrivedAcross 4` and `vertical 0 < ArrivedUp 3` with `final` → `Stop`;
   `speed == max_speed` so `Accelerate` is a no-op and the only thing that can zero `stuck_count` is
   `DetectStuck` reaching its reset. `stuck_count == 2` and the 231 predicate both pinned.
3. **Fly, no arrival** (new, the other direction, so the guard cannot be inverted or pushed into the
   arrival branch): waypoint 100 away so the command survives, `ContactCollided` set, `speed 5 >
   StuckSpeed 2`, `stuck_ticks 0 < window 16` → `stuck_ticks += 1` (the window counts **updates**,
   `ObjectMotion.Ticks = 1f`, not `Dt`) and `stuck_count` stays 0 because `HandleStuck` returns without
   `ContactStuck`.

```csharp
if (obj.Speed > targetSpeed)      obj.Speed = MathF.Max(obj.Speed - obj.Deceleration * Dt, targetSpeed);
else if (obj.Speed < targetSpeed) obj.Speed = MathF.Min(obj.Speed + obj.Acceleration * Dt, targetSpeed);
```

and it has exactly three callers: `MoveForward` (`:979`), `Walk` (`:819`) and `Fly` (`:840`).
The port had **inlined** it at all three sites. Review-21 F7 named that shape as the hazard,
and it is not a hypothetical one: batch 49 changed 2 of the 8 clamp sites and left the other 6
as `fminf`/`fmaxf`, which review-20 F2 caught. A fidelity fix applied to one copy and not the
others is invisible to every gate, because the copies are textually identical and no test
compares the arms with each other.

### What landed

`mdk_core/src/scripts/script_runtime.cpp` now has one file-scope free function,

```cpp
static void accelerate(MdkObject* obj, float targetSpeed) {
    if (obj->speed > targetSpeed) {
        obj->speed = mathMax(obj->speed - obj->deceleration * ScriptRuntime::kTick, targetSpeed);
    } else if (obj->speed < targetSpeed) {
        obj->speed = mathMin(obj->speed + obj->acceleration * ScriptRuntime::kTick, targetSpeed);
    }
}
```

called from `moveForward`, the walk arm and the fly arm. It is an ordinary concrete function
with the same file-scope-static shape as `detectStuck` next to it — no template, no virtual,
nothing §10 forbids. **Nothing in it is new arithmetic**: the two comparisons, the two clamps
and the multiply order are the lines that were already in all three arms, moved, so no
hot-path rule changes state (R3's float comparison is the oracle's own, relocated rather than
introduced; `gates_vfp` still reports `PASS blockers=0`).

`chase`'s clamp pair was **not** folded in, and its comment now says why: those two lines are
the C#'s own `Chase` formula (`ObjectMotion.cs:916-917`) — different constants, no
`MaxSpeed`/`TurnSpeedFactor` target, no `Dt` — so it is a second oracle function, not a fifth
copy of the first. Review-21 F7 counted it as a fourth copy; the oracle does not.

### The pin: `AccelerateIsOneImplementationAcrossTheArms` (`tests/scripts/vm_tests.cpp`)

17 rows × 3 arms. Each row poses the *same* movement state in each arm and runs one
`motionVelocity`, then asserts two things:

* every arm lands on the **same** speed — the property the collapse exists to hold; and
* that speed is the **oracle's, bit for bit**. The expected values are the IEEE-754 bits .NET
  10 prints from the private static `ObjectMotion.Accelerate` on the same inputs, read out of
  the oracle by reflection (probe mode `accel`, the same technique the `roll` mode already
  used for the private `Roll`). They are not the C++'s output.

Each arm is posed so its own target *is* the row's target: `MoveForward` takes `MaxSpeed` when
`MoveParameter` is non-zero; `Walk`/`Fly` take `MaxSpeed × TurnSpeedFactor(diff)`, which is
`MaxSpeed` with the waypoint straight ahead and `MaxSpeed × 0.5` with it 90° off. So the two
`half` rows hand those arms twice the target as `MaxSpeed` and pin, along with the step, the
factor the target came from. Every row also asserts the command survived (88/43/78), so an arm
that arrived and `Stop()`-ped cannot pass by leaving the speed untouched.

The oracle run (`mdkprobe 3 1 1 accel`, .NET 10, `/tmp/mdk-pi/obj3` — its `ObjectMotion.cs`
verified byte-identical to the repository's oracle):

```
ACCEL below           in=5/10/1/1        speed=5.0333333   bits=40A11111
ACCEL above           in=15/10/1/1       speed=14.966666   bits=416F7777
ACCEL equal           in=10/10/1/1       speed=10          bits=41200000
ACCEL overshoot_up    in=9.9/10/100/1    speed=10          bits=41200000
ACCEL overshoot_down  in=10.1/10/1/100   speed=10          bits=41200000
ACCEL zero_accel      in=5/10/0/0        speed=5           bits=40A00000
ACCEL negative_below  in=-2/10/1/1       speed=-1.9666667  bits=BFFBBBBC
ACCEL stop_to_zero    in=4/0/1/1         speed=3.9666667   bits=407DDDDE
ACCEL nan_accel_below in=5/10/NaN/1      speed=NaN         bits=7FC00000
ACCEL nan_decel_above in=15/10/1/NaN     speed=NaN         bits=7FC00000
ACCEL nan_speed       in=NaN/10/1/1      speed=NaN         bits=7FC00000
ACCEL nan_accel_above in=15/10/NaN/1     speed=14.966666   bits=416F7777
ACCEL nan_decel_below in=5/10/1/NaN      speed=5.0333333   bits=40A11111
ACCEL equal_nan_decel in=10/10/1/NaN     speed=10          bits=41200000
ACCEL equal_nan_accel in=10/10/NaN/1     speed=10          bits=41200000
```

Four of those rows are there specifically to make the *shape* of the branch unbreakable, and
each came out of the oracle rather than out of reasoning:

* `nan_accel_above` / `nan_decel_below` — the **comparison** picks the branch, not the clamp,
  so a NaN in the field the *other* branch reads must not touch the speed.
* `equal_nan_decel` / `equal_nan_accel` — both comparisons are **strict**, so at
  `Speed == target` neither branch runs and a NaN in either field stays out of the speed.
  Without these two rows, loosening `>` to `>=` is an equivalent mutant at every other row
  (`max(10 − 1/30, 10)` is still 10) and would have survived the table.

The `half` rows need no separate oracle row: the oracle takes the target directly, so their
expected bits are `below`'s and `above`'s.

| M3 | `moveForward` omits the step (an arm drifts by omission) | 26 | 12 rows |

| M6 | the helper's brake adds instead of subtracts | 15 | `above`, `overshoot_down`, `stop_to_zero`, `half_above`, `nan_accel_above` |
